learningObjective: Compute the effective cache-line utilization of a strided CPU access pattern and connect it to the arithmetic intensity seen by the memory system.

canonicalClaims.claim: Effective cache-line utilization equals useful bytes per line divided by cache-line size; hardware prefetchers do not reduce per-line waste, only latency to fetch the next line.
conditions: Each access lands in a distinct cache line (stride ≥ line size).
nonImplications: Does not imply the workload cannot be optimized; layout or tiling changes can restore stride-1 patterns.
Does not imply the CPU stalls; latency hiding can still be effective at high per-line waste.

misconceptions.claim: Hardware prefetching lifts effective per-line utilization to 100%.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Prefetching hides latency but does not change the number of bytes actually consumed from each line; wasted bytes are still transferred over the memory bus.

misconceptions.claim: Utilization is set by the SIMD lane width relative to the element width.
misconceptions.whyWrong: SIMD width is a compute-side property; cache-line utilization is a memory-side property (bytes fetched vs bytes used).

misconceptions.claim: Out-of-order execution improves cache-line utilization by issuing multiple loads per line.
misconceptions.whyWrong: OoO reorders independent operations to hide latency, but doesn't retroactively make more of a line 'useful' if the access pattern doesn't touch those bytes.

implementationFacts: Cache line 64 B; FP32 element 4 B; stride 16 elements = 64 B = exactly one line per element.
performanceScenarios: Row-major traversal of a column-major matrix produces stride-N access; layout transformations (transpose or blocking) restore utilization.
